AGA Survey: 82% of Americans Want Prediction Markets Regulated as Gambling

Published November 17, 2026 · 4 min read · By the OddsLighthouse Editorial Team

The American Gaming Association released its annual national survey this week, finding that 82% of registered voters believe prediction markets offering sports event contracts — platforms like Kalshi, Polymarket, and Crypto.com — should be regulated as gambling products rather than as financial instruments. The finding lands squarely in the middle of a yearlong legal and political fight over whether those platforms belong under state gaming regulation or federal commodities oversight.

What the survey found

The AGA's "American Attitudes Toward Gaming 2026" survey polled 2,268 registered voters age 21 and up between September 2 and 18, with a reported margin of error of about two percentage points. Support for treating prediction markets as gambling was consistent across party lines: 84% of Democrats, 82% of Republicans, and 80% of independents agreed. Roughly three-quarters of respondents said trading a sports event contract is fundamentally the same activity as placing a bet through a licensed sportsbook. Majorities also said they want the same consumer protections sportsbooks already follow applied to prediction markets, including age verification at 21, roughly 71% backing state-regulator licensing, and about 70% wanting the platforms to honor state self-exclusion lists for people who've asked to be barred from gambling.

The survey also flagged a notable information gap: roughly half of respondents said they believe prediction markets are already licensed and regulated the way traditional sportsbooks are, which isn't accurate — the platforms currently operate under Commodity Futures Trading Commission oversight and argue they're exempt from state gambling law entirely.

Why this fight is still unresolved

Kalshi and Polymarket maintain that their sports contracts are financial derivatives under the CFTC's exclusive federal authority, which they say preempts state and tribal gambling regulation. State regulators and attorneys general in multiple states have pushed back with cease-and-desist orders and lawsuits, and federal appeals courts have issued conflicting rulings on whether the Commodity Exchange Act actually preempts state gambling law — a split that has produced petitions asking the Supreme Court to resolve the question. The AGA, which represents commercial and tribal casino and sportsbook operators, has been among the most vocal critics of letting prediction markets offer what it considers sports betting without the licensing, taxation, and consumer-protection rules its own members follow.

Why it matters to US bettors

The dispute isn't just an industry turf war — it directly affects what protections are in place for someone placing a sports-related wager through a prediction market rather than a licensed sportsbook. Until the jurisdictional question is settled, protections that are standard at licensed books, such as mandatory self-exclusion honoring and strict age verification, aren't guaranteed to apply the same way on a prediction-market platform. The AGA's survey is likely to be cited by state regulators and in congressional debate as evidence of public appetite for closing that gap, though it doesn't itself change any law or regulation.
